text: Non-experimental estimators applied to the National Supported Work demonstration often failed to replicate the experimental estimates, even when they passed conventional specification tests.
LaLonde (1986, Table 5 notes) reports an experimental NSW effect on male participants' 1978 earnings of $886 (SE $476) in 1982 dollars.
Propensity-score stratification and matching applied to LaLonde's data produced estimates close to the experimental benchmark by using only comparison units similar to the treated.
Propensity-score matching selects comparable controls without using outcome information, and checking pre-treatment comparability is a central diagnostic.
Propensity-score matching estimates for the NSW data are highly sensitive to the variables included in the score and to the analysis sample; difference-in-differences matching performed best.

Dehejia (2005) argues that the propensity-score specification must be chosen separately for each treatment-comparison sample and that sensitivity to small changes in the specification should be examined.
Adjustment for the propensity score is sufficient to remove bias due to all observed covariates.
Under unconfoundedness and overlap, average treatment effects can be estimated by regression, matching, propensity-score weighting or blocking, and combinations of these.
Estimating the treatment's effect on a lagged outcome that it cannot have affected provides an indirect test of unconfoundedness.
Imbens and Wooldridge recommend reporting normalized differences in covariate means; differences above one quarter suggest linear regression will be sensitive to specification.
Weighting by the inverse of a nonparametrically estimated propensity score yields an efficient estimator of the average treatment effect.
Augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimators are doubly robust: consistent if either the treatment-assignment model or the outcome model is correctly specified.
Neyman-orthogonal scores combined with cross-fitting remove the bias from regularization and overfitting when nuisance functions are estimated by machine learning.
Imbens (2003) studies how sensitive program-evaluation estimates are to departures from the unconfoundedness assumption.
Limited overlap makes treatment-effect estimates imprecise and specification-sensitive; discarding units with estimated propensity scores outside [0.1, 0.9] approximates the optimal subsample.
The Benjamini-Hochberg step-up procedure controls the false discovery rate for independent test statistics and is more powerful than familywise error control.
Romano and Wolf's stepwise procedure controls the familywise error rate asymptotically while accounting for the dependence among test statistics.
Anderson (2008) combines summary-index tests with familywise error rate and false discovery rate corrections and recommends declaring the family of tests in advance.
A pre-analysis plan prevented cherry-picking among many outcome indicators; without it, two divergent and equally erroneous interpretations could have been produced.
Pre-specifying and reporting all planned analyses greatly reduces data-mining problems, though pre-analysis plans also have costs and limits.
Pre-analysis plans can be credibly applied to observational research when they are registered before the researcher can access the data.
Failure to reject a point null can be highly informative, and non-significant results should be reported and discussed visibly.
Across more than 200 evaluations of active labor market programs, average impacts are close to zero in the short run and become more positive two to three years after program completion.

rob-diff74 (ATT on re78 - re74 under conditional parallel trends 1974-1978; a different estimand and assumption) rejects a zero effect at 5% (95% CI excludes 0: true). Its bias has no sign known in advance: upward if enrolees' 1974 earnings were already transitorily depressed, downward if their lower earnings reflect a permanently lower growth path; it is not a defence of the primary and does not trigger the disagreement rule.
rob-diff74 fails the H1b equivalence criterion: its 90% CI is not inside (-M, M) (it lies entirely below -M: true). Reported next to its estimate; it does not trigger the disagreement rule.

Sensitivity statement required by the plan's reading rule: none of the conclusions (robustness to a shift of the estimate by M, the H1 non-rejection, and the H1b equivalence) is robust to an unobserved confounder as strong as earnings75 (1975 earnings, its square and the 1975 no-earnings indicator), which would move the estimate by up to 1,716 dollars; the result could be produced by unobserved selection of that strength, and an unobserved 1976 earnings shock is plausibly at least that strongly related to enrolment. The equivalence conclusion (H1b) is also not robust to a confounder as strong as earnings74 (|bias| 204 against an equivalence-ending shift of 181). This statement must accompany H1b wherever it is stated, the abstract included.
Smallest diagonal R2 (R2_D = R2_Y) of an unobserved binary confounder that moves the estimate by a shift of M in the Imbens (2003) model.
Sensitivity target for a shift of M, nominal dollars.

Reading rule, target margin (t = 483.5): robust to 8 of 9 benchmark groups. Groups are ranked by the larger |bias| of the two signs of delta at each group's benchmark point (an implementation choice fixed in code before any outcome was read; the plan does not fix the ordering). Robust to (|bias| in dollars, strongest first): earn74 (203.8), age (128.3), educ (126.1), married (6.1), health (5.8), urban (4.6), children (0.8), region (0.0). Not robust to (weakest first): earn75 (1,716.5). Strongest robust: earn74; weakest not robust: earn75; earnings75: NOT robust.

Groups are ranked by the larger |bias| of the two signs of delta at each group's benchmark point (an implementation choice fixed in code before any outcome was read; the plan does not fix the ordering). Robust to (|bias| in dollars, strongest first): age (128.3), educ (126.1), married (6.1), health (5.8), urban (4.6), children (0.8), region (0.0). Not robust to (weakest first): earn74 (203.8), earn75 (1,716.5). Strongest robust: age; weakest not robust: earn74; earnings75: NOT robust. Under ranking by R2_D instead, educ (R2_D 0.024) would outrank age (R2_D 0.010) as the strongest robust group; their |bias| values are nearly tied.
